title: What Do History Majors Do? - University of New Hampshire
content: Are you fascinated with how things used to be and what that means for us now? History is the study of the past and how that knowledge can inform the present and the future. This is a broad degree program, allowing you to focus on a particular country, region, time period, or aspect of human culture that interests you, such as religion, science, or cultural movements. You’ll develop the skills in critical reading and writing that form the basis of a solid liberal arts education and prepare you for a wide range of careers, as well as graduate or professional school. Meet William Kirkpatrick '26, a history major from Eliot, Maine, who has found a close community on the UNH campus, with plenty of room to explore by studying how dinosaur bones may have influenced Greek mythology and by studying abroad in Turkey. William Kirkpatrick: I chose UNH because the campus has the appeal of the beautiful small schools of New England while providing enough opportunities, classes, and people to feel like a significant step up from my small Maine high school. Growing up with two parents who worked at UNH, I also had the opportunity to meet some of the professors, faculty, and staff, all of whom were extremely kind and welcoming. It seemed like an easy choice. My favorite thing about COLA is that almost every class I took during my first three years allowed me to explore topics I had never considered before. Coming in my first year, I certainly didn't think I would write a final paper two years later comparing Odysseus in Homer's "The Odyssey" to Mad Max. I can't think of another college that would actively encourage such ambitions. "Almost every class I took during my first three years allowed me to explore topics I had never considered before." I love the history department because of the many subjects it offers. One class will have me writing about medieval hunting practices, and the next will provide the opportunity to present about why dinosaur bones have heavily influenced Greek mythology. I believe, above all, that my liberal arts education has given me the ability to think critically and present my thoughts in a convincing manner after considering the presented material. Paraphrasing Professor Gregory McMahon, a liberal arts education is a lesson in persuasion, critical thinking, and independence presented in the most fascinating way possible. I agree! "I believe, above all, that my liberal arts education has given me the ability to think critically and present my thoughts in a convincing manner." My most impactful professors are both Professor Gregory McMahon and Professor David Bachrach. During my first semester freshman year, Professor Bachrach taught me how to write like a historian and encouraged me to reach out to him with drafts of all my papers. I still refer to some of my papers from that year for format and grammar. Then, in my sophomore year, Professor McMahon helped me understand how fun it is to create new ideas based on ancient sources and supported me when I would come to him with frankly crazy ideas for papers. Professor McMahon sent me to study abroad on his archaeological dig in Turkey this summer. I never took people who said that studying abroad would change your life seriously, because how could it? However, my time in Turkey is one of the highlights of my college experience and probably my life. It's such a vastly different culture from ours, but I fit right in since everyone I met treated me as if they had known me their whole life. In addition to the amazing Turkish culture, getting to see, touch, and excavate the artifacts that I've spent so much of my college career reading about, analyzing, and writing about is a once-in-a-lifetime experience that I can hopefully turn into a twice-in-a-lifetime experience in the near future. "I never took people who said that studying abroad would change your life seriously, because how could it? However, my time in Turkey is one of the highlights of my college experience and probably my life." I received the Trustee's Scholarship coming in my freshman year. This scholarship allowed me to free up money to study abroad in Turkey this summer. I will be forever grateful that UNH allowed me the opportunity to experience Turkish culture from a perspective that many people are not afforded. There are two pieces of advice I would give my freshman self. The first is to explore the campus earlier. There are many cool areas, such as College Woods, the Fishbowl, and the tennis courts, that I never really used until later on. UNH is meant to be explored, and everyone has their favorite spot on campus to study and hang out. The second piece is to study abroad earlier. If I had the chance to go on a second trip before graduation, I would have taken it immediately. I was originally scared that I would feel alone, homesick, and out of place, but I found the opposite was true. There will never be another opportunity to experience international culture like that offered in college, so why not take it? I have found a sense of community within my friend group. Most of us met during the "Become the Roar" tradition during orientation, and we have stayed very close friends throughout all four years. My freshman year roommate is still my best friend, and all of us shared an eight-person suite in Mills Hall during my sophomore year. One thing people might be surprised to learn about me is that during the summers, I work as a groundskeeper for my local cemetery. After someone learns this, I am immediately asked if I bury the people, too, which, yes, I do. However, I am hopefully far from the cemetery groundskeeper stereotype. title: Vermonters back 2nd-home tax, divided on school consolidation, safe injection sites, according to UNH poll - WCAX
content:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - Vermonters strongly support placing a new tax on second homes, but are divided on school consolidation and safe injection sites, according to a new poll by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center. In the poll, 78% of respondents say they support a tax on homes that are not the primary residence of property owners, while 15% oppose it. Legislation with bipartisan backing is expected to be taken up by the Legislature next year. School consolidation dominated the last biennium, with lawmakers pulling back from mandatory mergers. But nearly half of Vermonters continue to favor school district consolidation, even if that leads to school closures. The poll found 49% support the idea of lowering education costs, while 39% are opposed. Harm reduction methods, like safe injection sites, have also been a focal point in Burlington. The survey shows Vermonters at large are divided over opening a site where drug use happens under the supervision of medical professionals, with 39% in favor and 43% opposed. title: UNH Researcher Lends Expertise to Help Outline Priorities in U.S. Climate Assessment - University of New Hampshire
content: Serita Frey, professor of natural resources and the environment at UNH, is a co-author of the commentary “Research priorities for robust climate assessments in the United States.” The paper brings together 175 authors across the United States to outline research priorities that can inform future national, regional, local, sectoral and topical climate assessments. The commentary was published in the journals Earth’s Future and Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society. It is the first paper in the U.S. Climate Collection: Informing Assessment of Risks and Solutions—a joint special collection of the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society that will publish U.S.-focused climate assessment science and research synthesis papers that can inform future national and sub-national assessments. Frey contributed to the commentary through leading the section on forests which identifies key research priorities for understanding how U.S. forests are responding to climate change, including the effects of warming, drought, wildfire, pests, and other disturbances. It also highlights the need to better quantify the role of forests in carbon storage and climate mitigation, while supporting biodiversity and ecosystem services. “As climate risks intensify, forests will play an increasingly important role in carbon storage, biodiversity conservation, and community resilience," says Frey. “This paper identifies key research priorities needed to ensure that future climate assessments capture both the vulnerabilities of forests and their potential to help address climate change.” The commentary identifies assessment opportunities and research needs across planetary-scale systems, environmental settings, economic sectors, U.S. regions and U.S. international interests. Across these areas, the authors identify several cross-cutting priorities for research synthesis, including how greenhouse gas emissions continue to alter and amplify climate hazards; how compounding extremes and cascading risks are straining legacy policies, infrastructure, and institutions; how social systems shape both climate impacts and responses; and how future assessments should evaluate mitigation, adaptation, disaster management, climate interventions and resilience planning and implementation decisions as a climate action portfolio. Scientific assessments synthesize complex bodies of evidence so households, communities, businesses, institutions and governments can make informed decisions as climate hazards intensify. The most recent U.S. National Climate Assessment was published in 2023; scientific understanding has advanced since then, and climate assessments are continuing by states, localities and businesses. The commentary argues that the pace of assessment and the integration of science with decision-making must accelerate as climate impacts continue to grow. title: UNH Stock Tracks Hot Monthly Streak: Wall Street Cheers ‘Impressive’ Q2 And Sees Over 20% More Room To Run - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth Group, Inc. (UNH) are headed for their fourth monthly win as Wall Street turns more bullish after a large second-quarter (Q2) earnings beat and a sweeping increase to its 2026 outlook. UNH stock rose 1% on Friday, bringing its monthly gain to nearly 3%, while shares also finished the week marginally higher. BofA called UnitedHealth’s quarter “impressive,” noting that earnings beat consensus by 31% and guidance rose 12%. The firm raised its price target to $512, implying over 20% upside, while reiterating a ‘Buy’ rating and citing a “strong” quarter and broad-based outlook increase. Morgan Stanley was even more bullish, lifting its target to $529, implying a 24% upside. The firm said the Q2 beat and higher 2026 targets “validate its disciplined strategy and establish a stronger base for future growth.” Truist, Oppenheimer and KeyBanc each moved to $500 targets, implying a 17% upside. Truist highlighted top- and bottom-line beats, a better Medical Care Ratio, and improving expectations for UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health. Oppenheimer said that the company “handily” topped expectations, while KeyBanc said results “topped bullish expectations” and argued UnitedHealth could hit $30 in earnings per share (EPS) sooner than anticipated. Goldman Sachs and UBS both raised their targets to $490, implying a 15% upside. Goldman cited a “material” earnings beat, stronger Optum Health profitability and a larger-than-expected guidance increase. UBS said UnitedHealth was “making good progress with more to go.” Meanwhile, RBC Capital raised its target to $478, implying a 12% upside. It remained positive on the earnings beat and guidance hike but flagged investor concern around persistent commercial medical-cost pressure. UnitedHealth posted adjusted EPS of $6.38, beating the $4.92 consensus and rising from $4.08 a year ago. Revenue of $112.03 billion also topped estimates, while the medical care ratio improved to 86.7% from 89.4%. Additionally, the company raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to $19.50-$20 from more than $18.25, lifted UnitedHealthcare’s operating profit forecast to at least $12 billion, and increased Optum Health’s outlook to at least $2.2 billion. CEO Stephen Hemsley said UnitedHealth was “returning to form” as stronger performance disciplines took hold. He reaffirmed the company’s 13%-16% long-term earnings-growth target and doubled the 2026 buyback goal to at least $5 billion. Medicare Advantage drove the beat, with costs coming in below expectations. “Medicare delivered a strong second quarter,” UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said. Commercial plans remained the weak spot, with medical-cost trends above 11%. On the other hand, Optum said its tools added nearly 200,000 patient-facing hours, cut clinician cognitive burnout by 90%, and achieved a 96% first-pass approval rate for digital prior authorizations. SpaceX (SPCX) shares rose 1% overnight heading into Monday after CEO Elon Musk dismissed a report claiming that the rocket and satellite company had placed a $52 billion order with Foxconn for Nvidia-powered AI servers. SPCX stock fell 5% on Friday, extending its weekly decline to 15%. “This is fake news,” Musk said on X in response to a post summarizing the reported agreement. Taiwan’s Economic Daily said that Hon Hai Precision Industry, better known as Foxconn, had secured its first contract to manufacture AI servers for SpaceX. According to the report, SpaceX was preparing to deploy more than 13,000 server racks built around Nvidia’s GB300 platform. The estimated $52 billion value was based on an assumed cost of $4 million per rack rather than a disclosed contract price. Citrini analyst Jukan said on X that Foxconn had displaced the dominance of Dell Technologies and Super Micro Computer in supplying AI server infrastructure to SpaceX. It also claimed deliveries would begin in late 2026 and continue into the first quarter of 2027. Chairman Young Liu has previously said Foxconn expects to capture more than 40% of the global AI server market, while shipments of advanced AI racks are projected to increase through the end of the year. A separate Wall Street Journal report on Friday said that SpaceX was in discussions with the U.S. Department of Defense about supplying data-center capacity worth several billion dollars for military AI workloads. The talks were said to be ongoing and could still fail to produce an agreement. SpaceX has also explored offering computing power to outside AI customers as it seeks to compete more directly with cloud infrastructure providers such as CoreWeave. In June, SpaceX also reached computing arrangements with Google and Anthropic. The Google deal covered access to about 110,000 Nvidia chips, while Anthropic secured capacity at the company’s Colossus 1 data center in Memphis. The potential Defense Department arrangement would deepen SpaceX’s already extensive relationship with the U.S. military. The Pentagon relies on the company for rocket launches, satellite communications and missile-tracking systems. It is also seeking more computing capacity as intelligence agencies and military units increase their use of AI. SpaceX employees have reportedly discussed selling computing capacity at prices designed to compete with established cloud and specialized AI infrastructure providers. The Pentagon, meanwhile, is seeking funding for a new AI Arsenal initiative centered on access to high-end chips and computing resources. The military has also approved multiple tech companies, including SpaceX, Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle, for classified AI-related work. Korean stocks tumbled again on Monday, led by declines in chip giants Samsung and SK Hynix, setting the stage for another bout of the recent yo-yo trade, where weakness in Korean chip stocks spills over to U.S. semiconductor names and back again, ahead of a key week of U.S. tech earnings. South Korea’s Kospi as well as Samsung stock fell 4.3% each, while SK Hynix shares were down 4% in local afternoon time. The two stocks together account for roughly 60% of the Kospi’s market capitalization, making it one of the most concentrated major equity indices in the world. SK Hynix's U.S. listed stock declined 0.3% in the overnight session. As of the last close, they have declined by about 10% from the opening price on the first day of trading on Jul. 10. The Direxion Daily South Korea Bull 3X Shares (KORU), a three-times leveraged ETF tracking South Korea’s largest stocks, was down 2%. U.S. memory stocks Micron and SanDisk were holding in the green, rebounding after a dismal weekly performance. Citigroup on Monday downgraded the South Korean market to “neutral,” ending an overweight stance held since mid-2025 due to heightened market volatility, according to a report in South China Morning Post. The move was driven by extreme volatility in chip stocks and a reduced exposure to AI-themed trades. The firm added that it remains long-term bullish on AI, but has turned more cautious on Korea in the near term. Since the start of July, investors have been rotating out of semiconductor and AI infrastructure names and back into large-cap technology and software stocks, marking a shift after months of chip-led gains. Memory makers such as Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix, along with other AI hardware suppliers, have come under pressure as investors question whether the explosive AI infrastructure spending can continue at the same pace. Meanwhile, money has flowed into software and Big Tech names – including Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta – as investors seek companies that are better positioned to monetize AI through applications and services rather than infrastructure alone. The rotation also reflects profit-taking in richly valued chip stocks ahead of earnings season. Alphabet will be the first of the tech majors to report this season, with its announcement scheduled for Wednesday, followed by Intel the next day. GOOGL has gained 11% year to date, while INTC rallied 156%, underscoring how investors piled into chip stocks in 2026. Investors will closely watch for signs that AI-driven demand remains resilient and whether company outlooks justify the sector’s outsized gains. ARK Investment Management founder-CEO Cathie Wood cheered Eli Lilly’s $3.8 billion AtaiBeckley acquisition on Sunday, calling it a “well-deserved” payoff for shareholders and a validation of Christian Angermayer’s psychedelic vision. ATAI stock rose 1% on Friday, adding 40% over the past five sessions and marking its best week in more than a year. Shares, however, were dipping more than 1% in overnight trading heading into Monday. Wood highlighted on X the biotech company’s role in bringing psychedelic medicines closer to mainstream clinical use: “Not only a well-deserved return for ATAI shareholders, this transaction validates Christian’s heartfelt mission and vision,” Wood said. She called Angermayer’s work with ATAI “one of the biggest catalysts of the psychedelic renaissance,” adding that clinical trials are increasingly validating the potential of psychedelics in treatment-resistant depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and broader mental health conditions. Wood also credited Angermayer with backing the field long before psychedelic medicine became widely accepted, fashionable, or investable. “Long before psychedelics were accepted, fashionable, or investable, Christian’s life’s mission was to reactivate them and bring back hope and health for those who had lost both,” she said. Wood’s praise came after ARK Invest reduced its ATAI stake last week. The ARK Genomic Revolution ETF (ARKG) sold 1.12 million ATAI shares worth about $6.02 million. As of Friday, however, ARKG still held 3.19 million shares valued at $22.78 million, or 1.4% of the fund. Lilly was also ARKG’s seventh-largest holding, with 61,258 shares worth $71.62 million and a 4.4% weighting. Eli Lilly said last week that it would acquire AtaiBeckley for up to $3.8 billion for the psychedelic drug developer as it builds out its neuroscience pipeline. Under the deal, shareholders would receive $6.75 in cash per ATAI share, with Lilly committing $2.8 billion at closing and an additional $1 billion for future milestones. The deal marked a 26% premium to AtaiBeckley’s shareholders. The companies are targeting completion of the acquisition in the third quarter of 2026. The centerpiece of the deal is BPL-003, an intranasal psychedelic therapy being tested in late-stage studies for treatment-resistant depression. Jefferies has projected that the drug could eventually generate $1 billion to $2 billion in sales if the program succeeds. AtaiBeckley has said the first late-stage data are expected in early 2029. Angermayer reflected on the deal over the weekend in an X post, saying ATAI’s next phase is about commercialization rather than advocacy. “Ten years ago, psychedelics needed an evangelist. Today, they need commercialization,” he said. After first exploring psychedelics in 2014, Angermayer helped launch Compass Pathways and ATAI in 2017 and invested more than $100 million of his own capital in ATAI. The two companies later raised over $1.5 billion, went public and helped build clinical credibility for psychedelic medicine. title: UNH Vs. HUM: Which Insurer Stock Has More Upside After CMS Reverses Wall Street’s Biggest Medicare Rate Fear? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth, Inc. (UNH) and Humana, Inc. (HUM) are back in the spotlight on Tuesday after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) lifted Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, with Wall Street estimates pointing to a clear frontrunner. UNH stock rose 8% in extended trading, while HUM stock gained 11%. Over the past year, however, UNH has fallen about 45% and HUM nearly 27%, with both stocks underperforming the broader Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLV), which climbed 10% over the same period. The CMS finalized a 2.48% increase in Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, up from the January proposal that kept rates roughly flat and wiped out nearly $100 billion in market value across major insurers. The updated policy is expected to add more than $13 billion in additional funding to Medicare Advantage plans next year, the CMS said. With the policy overhang removed, attention has shifted back to valuation targets, which point to higher implied upside for UnitedHealth than for Humana. Based on Koyfin estimates, UnitedHealth carries a 12-month average price target of $357.81, implying a 27% upside from the stock’s last close. Coverage across 29 analysts includes 7 ‘Strong Buy’, 16 ‘Buy’, 4 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this month, Raymond James upgraded the stock to ‘Outperform’ with a $330 price target, citing potential upside from expense trends and expected margin improvement at Optum Health, the company’s care delivery arm. Meanwhile, Bernstein SocGen Group reiterated an ‘Outperform’ rating with a $405 target, pointing to UnitedHealth’s expanding AI strategy. The company recently launched its generative AI companion, Avery, as part of broader efforts to reduce operating costs across its insurance segment, where it plans nearly $1 billion in expense cuts and is closing or divesting about 550 Optum Health clinics. UnitedHealth also expects to lose as many as 2.8 million insurance members this year, with revenue potentially declining for the first time since the 1980s as longtime chair and former CEO Stephen Hemsley leads a turnaround effort. The stock still remains below the level at which Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway built its stake last year and faces scrutiny over Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment practices following a Senate committee review. Humana’s upside appears more modest based on Koyfin estimates, with a 12-month average price target of $212.17, implying a 16% upside from current levels. Among 27 covering analysts, the stock carries 2 ‘Strong Buy’, 6 ‘Buy’, 17 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this year, the company projected adjusted 2026 earnings of at least $9 per share, below consensus expectations of $11.87, while the insurer said margins in its individual Medicare Advantage business could remain just below break-even this year. Several brokerages subsequently lowered price targets, with UBS and BofA maintaining ‘Neutral’ ratings after Humana’s 2026 EPS outlook came in roughly 24% below consensus. On the other hand, Morgan Stanley warned that uncertainty around the size of Humana’s 2026 membership cohort remains a risk “particularly heading into 2027 and beyond.” Cantor Fitzgerald said the stock may remain range-bound until clearer membership data emerges in the second quarter, and Guggenheim said it was taking “a prudent view” of the company’s 2027 earnings outlook. Still, Humana expects enrollment in its individual Medicare Advantage plans to increase about 25% in 2026 compared with last year, with over 70% of new members coming from competing plans. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for UNH and HUM was ‘extremely bullish’ amid ‘extremely high’ message volume. One user said UNH “was $600 a year ago. One of the safest blue chips to double In a couple years.” Another user noted that “this $13B increase provides critical revenue relief, offsetting rising medical costs and securing sector stability.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Shares of Hologic (HOLX), Kosmos Energy (KOS) and Marvell Technology (MRVL) touched fresh 52-week highs on Monday, driven by oil-price strength, momentum in AI and fresh dealmaking. Last week, Marvell shares rose 13%, Kosmos Energy edged up about 0.3%, and Hologic ended marginally lower. Hologic shares gained as investors positioned ahead of the company’s planned April 7 takeover by investment firms Blackstone and TPG, after the company said it had received all required regulatory approvals. The deal, first announced in October 2025, values the company at up to $79 per share and $18.3 billion in enterprise value. The company also said its chairman, president and CEO Steve MacMillan plans to retire when the transaction closes. Separately, Casey's General Stores is set to replace Hologic in the S&P 500 index on Thursday as the company prepares to exit public markets following the acquisition. Kosmos Energy shares benefited from rising crude prices amid geopolitical tensions tied to the U.S.-Iran conflict, which lifted sentiment across energy companies. The rally was also buoyed by several analyst upgrades. Last month, Johnson Rice upgraded the stock to ‘Buy’ with a $4.25 price target, while Goldman Sachs raised its price target to $2.25. Bernstein said conflicts that extend beyond the early stages “could typically last for years,” adding that given the “uncertainty and right tail risk,” the firm continues to recommend adding exposure to energy. Separately, Mizuho raised its 2026 oil-price outlook by 14% to $73.25 per barrel, saying it was “too early to say whether the conflict raises the structural price of global oil,” but that the bias is “likely higher.” In February, Kosmos agreed to sell its stake in Equatorial Guinea production assets to Panoro Energy for up to $219.5 million, which CEO Andrew Inglis said would “enhance liquidity and accelerate debt reduction” while allowing the company to focus capital on higher-value assets. Meanwhile, Marvell shares jumped after expanding a partnership with Nvidia through the NVLink Fusion ecosystem, boosting the company’s position in next-generation AI infrastructure. Nvidia also disclosed a $2 billion investment in Marvell. Separately, Erste Group initiated coverage of Marvell with a ‘Buy’ rating, citing continued profit growth, improving return on equity and strong positioning in optical DSP and custom silicon used in AI systems. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for HOLX and MRVL was ‘bullish’ late Monday, with message volume ‘extremely high’ for HOLX and ‘normal’ for MRVL, while KOS sentiment was ‘neutral’ amid ‘normal’ message volume. So far this year, HOLX shares are up about 2%, KOS has surged 242%, and MRVL has gained 29%. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. U.S. stock futures traded lower late Monday as traders tracked U.S. President Donald Trump’s deadline for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while weighing ceasefire talks amid elevated oil prices. As of 10.15 p.m. ET, Nasdaq 100 futures were down 0.8%, while S&P 500 futures were down by 0.6%. Dow futures were down 0.4%. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment toward the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) and Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) was ‘extremely bearish’ amid ‘high’ message volume, and sentiment toward the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) was ‘bearish’ amid ‘normal’ message volume. Speaking at a White House conference on Monday, Trump reiterated that the U.S. military could target Iranian bridges and power plants if the strait is not reopened by 8 p.m. ET Tuesday. He said negotiations were “going well,” but added that restoring access through Hormuz remains a “very big priority.” He also said that while he would like the U.S. to “take the oil,” Americans ultimately want U.S. forces to return home. The U.S., Iran and regional mediators are reportedly exploring a possible 45-day ceasefire that could open the door to a settlement, while Washington and Tehran are also supposedly reviewing a Pakistan-brokered proposal to restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. However, Tehran has said it would only accept ceasefire terms that include a permanent end to the war, sanctions relief, reconstruction commitments and guarantees around safe navigation through the strait. It also warned that strikes on civilian infrastructure could trigger retaliatory attacks on energy facilities across the Gulf. The conflict, now in its sixth week, continues to ripple through energy markets, with West Texas Intermediate settling near $112.41 per barrel and Brent crude closing around $109.77. Michael Cembalest, chair of market and investment strategy at J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management, said that the belief the U.S. economy is insulated from a closure of the Strait of Hormuz is “mostly false,” adding that U.S. fossil-fuel independence “is not as much of an economic firewall as you might think.” In the previous session, the S&P 500 logged its fourth straight session of gains, marking its longest winning streak since January: Investors also weighed weaker-than-expected economic data, with the U.S. services sector expanding at a slower pace in March. The ISM services index fell 2.1 points to 54, with employment posting its sharpest drop since 2023. Broadcom (AVGO): Shares rose 2% in extended trading after the company announced a long-term agreement with Alphabet’s Google to develop and supply next-generation Tensor Processing Units and expand AI infrastructure partnership through 2031 alongside Anthropic. Enovix (ENVX): Shares posted their best session in nine months on Monday as retail traders speculated about a potential catalyst after Chinese media reported a deal with AR-optics firm MoJie to improve battery life in AI-enabled smart glasses. Humana (HUM), UnitedHealth Group (UNH), Elevance Health (ELV): Shares of health insurers rallied in extended trading after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) finalized a 2.48% increase in Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, expected to add more than $13 billion in plan funding. In broader markets, the yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note hovered near 4.33%, its highest level in about a week. Gold steadied near $4,664 per ounce after a two-day slide, while silver traded around $73.18. Asian markets were mostly higher on Tuesday, with the MSCI Asia-Pacific index excluding Japan rising about 0.4%. Shares opened higher in Australia, while Japan opened lower. Among the catalysts for Tuesday are durable-goods orders, durable-goods orders excluding transportation, remarks from Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, consumer credit data, and comments from Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson. Algorhythm Holdings, Inc. shares fell 7.1% on Monday, extending losses for a second straight session despite the AI logistics firm reporting upbeat results. Still, retail sentiment turned bullish, with many traders viewing the dip as a buying opportunity. Algorhythm Holdings has emerged as one of the key stocks on retail traders’ radar after it more than tripled in a single day in mid-February. Although it has lost most of those gains, interest remains high with Stocktwits watcher count increasing by nearly 20% in the past quarter. Retail sentiment for RIME was ‘bullish’ as of late Monday, up from ‘bearish’ on Thursday (Friday was a market holiday due to Good Friday). “I still see $RIME with a strong run up despite the low volume drop today. I’ll be loading another tranche tomorrow on this one if it stays depressed another day,” a user said. In another post, they shared the stock chart, which showed a breakout pattern building. Another user wrote: “This will pop soon!  Earnings were decent given the stage of the company.  Rev increased and cost went down... Expect a $3-5 pop! To be sure, RIME has rebounded nearly 30% from its March 30 low, which sits near the stock’s all-time bottom. Algorhythm Holdings reported fourth-quarter and full-year results in the early hours of April 2. Revenue rocketed 1,367%, to $4.4 million last year, primarily due to the acquisition of SemiCab India (SMCB Solutions), which concluded in May. Net loss declined 32%, to $16.6 million. With the acquisition of SemiCab, an AI-driven logistics platform that optimizes trucking networks, Algorhythm Holdings has effectively pivoted into a new business. Earlier, it sold karaoke machines and audio equipment. The SemiCab business achieved an annualized run rate of $10 million last year, thanks to five new contract wins with some of the largest multinational fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) companies in India and six contract expansions, the company said in its results statement. In the new year, it has added Coca-Cola India and MTR Foods as new clients. Algorhythm Holdings added that it cut its operating expenses by 20% and reduced liabilities by almost 50% in 2025, and would further improve its balance sheet this year. (TSLA) flashed fresh warning signals on Monday after slipping below key levels following a first-quarter (Q1) delivery miss, with one analyst projecting nearly 40% downside by June as bearish calls built after JPMorgan flagged a major downside to the stock. TSLA stock fell more than 2% on Monday, marking its lowest level in nearly seven months. GLJ Research analyst Gordon Johnson said on X that Tesla has broken below its 20, 50 and 75-day moving averages and remains trapped in a descending channel that began after the stock’s December highs near $480. He added that Fibonacci levels point to $322 as the next key support, while momentum indicators indicate the stock is not yet oversold. Johnson said investors should watch the $322- $346 range for a potential bounce. The analyst also said that, assuming consensus expectations for negative $1.6 billion in first-quarter free cash flow prove accurate and that prior correlations between Tesla’s free cash flow performance and its share price continue to hold, the stock could fall to $224-$269 by June 30, implying a 24%-36% downside from current levels. He also noted that Tesla’s car sales declined year-over-year in both 2024 and 2025 and are expected to fall again in 2026. “$TSLA has made literally NO PROGRESS on ‘robotaxis’ since launching in Austin in June of last yr. It could fall another 70-80%, and STILL be massively overvalued,” Johnson said, adding that the stock trades as 288x estimated 2026 earnings versus 31x for the Magnificent Seven. Johnson’s technical warning follows a bearish update from JPMorgan analyst Ryan Brinkman, who reiterated an ‘Underweight’ rating and set a $145 price target after Tesla’s Q1 delivery report, implying a 60% downside to current levels. “We ... advise investors approach TSLA shares with a high degree of caution,” Brinkman said. He also lowered 2026 earnings per share (EPS) estimate to $1.8 from $2, below consensus expectations, citing risks to demand, execution and competition as Tesla expands into lower-priced, higher-volume vehicle segments. Future Fund Managing Partner Gary Black said on X, “TSLA bulls out in full force today attacking Ryan Brinkman the person. Yes he’s been wrong on TSLA for 10 years, but he’s been right on TSLA the past five years, so has some credibility.” Separately, Jim Cramer called the bearish JPMorgan call “bold” and speculated that it “must mean people are going to sell this one to buy SpaceX.” His comment follows reports that SpaceX has confidentially filed for a U.S. initial public offering that could become the largest IPO on record, with the company reportedly valued at about $1.75 trillion. Tesla delivered 358,023 vehicles globally in the first quarter, missing Wall Street expectations for a second straight quarter. Deliveries rose 6% from the previous year but fell 14% from a quarter ago, marking the company’s weakest quarter since 2022 outside a Model Y production adjustment period. The company produced 408,386 vehicles during the quarter. Model 3 and Model Y deliveries totaled 341,893 units, while Model S, Model X and Cybertruck deliveries reached 16,130 units. Tesla also deployed 8.8 gigawatt-hours of energy-storage products, down from 10.4 gigawatt-hours a year earlier and below estimates. The results come as the U.S. electric-vehicle market adjusts to the phase-out of federal purchase incentives and competition from Chinese automakers intensifies across markets. Even as bearish calls emerged after the delivery miss, Baird maintained an ‘Outperform’ rating and lowered its price target to $538 from $548, still implying a 52% upside from the stock’s last close, according to an Investing report. Meanwhile, Canaccord Genuity reiterated a ‘Buy’ rating and maintained its $420 price target, representing a 19% upside from current levels following the delivery update. The brokerage noted that rising gasoline prices and firmer domestic used-Tesla pricing could support future demand. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for Tesla slipped to ‘extremely bearish’ from ‘bearish’ levels over the past day amid a 490% jump in 24-hour message volumes. One user said, “I think Tesla sees mid to low $200s into SpaceX taking the attention/crown. I kind of agree with JPM thesis this morning.” Another user claimed that TSLA is “eventually a $40 stock.” TSLA stock has tanked 22% so far this year, ranking as the second-worst performer among the “Magnificent Seven” group of equities. Shares of insurers UnitedHealth Group (UNH), Centene (CNC), Humana (HUM), and Elevance Health (ELV) jumped in Monday’s extended trading hours after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that the payments to private insurers offering Medicare Advantage plans will increase 2.48% next year. This increase implies $13 billion in additional payments to Medicare insurers for the year, the agency said. “When accounting for estimated risk score trend in MA due to factors such as population changes and coding practices, this amounts to a 4.98% increase,” the agency added. The move came as a surprise since in January, the CMS had proposed a roughly flat increase in payments for private Medicare plans the following year, sending shares of insurers down and wiping out about $100 billion in stock market value. The announcement further comes as a relief to the industry plagued by concerns over rising medical costs. Shares of UNH, CNC, HUM and ELV rallied between 5% and 11% at the time of writing. Shares of Aetna parent CVS Health (CVS) rose by about 6.5% while Molina Healthcare (MOH) stock rose a modest 3%. While UnitedHealth is the largest provider of private Medicare Advantage plans in the U.S., Humana is the second largest. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around UNH stock rose from ‘bullish’ to ‘extremely bullish’ territory over the past 24 hours, while message volume increased from ‘normal’ to ‘high’ levels. Sentiment around HUM stock, meanwhile, increased from ‘neutral’ to ‘extremely bullish’ territory over the past 24 hours, while message volume rose from ‘normal’ to ‘extremely high’ levels. A Stocktwits user expressed hopes for Wall Street analysts weighing in on the impact of the rate on UNH stock on Tuesday. Yet another user noted that analysts were expecting a lower rate. While UNH stock fell 46% over the past 12 months, HUM stock fell 28%. content: Get the best experience and stay connected to your community with our Spectrum News app. Learn More Get hyperlocal forecasts, radar and weather alerts. AUGUSTA — Another new poll on the race for U.S. Senate shows a statistical tie between Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson. The University of New Hampshire Survey Center pegs Jackson at 51% and Collins at 47%, results the pollsters describe as essentially a tie because of the margin of error. And just like the New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Sienna survey released early Thursday, the UNH poll was in the field before a ProPublica story critical of Collins posted on Tuesday. That NYT poll shows Collins at 49% and Jackson at 46%. The UNH poll, conducted between Sept. 17-21, also asked voters about the race for governor, which features Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett. Results put Pingree at 48%, Charles at 40% and Bennett at 5%. Another interesting result comes from Maine voters’ views on outgoing Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat finishing up her final year in office. The poll shows 57% disapproving of the way she handled the job as governor, 41% approving and 2% unsure. One of Mills’ key initiatives in the last year, issuing $300 “affordability checks” to many Mainers, also earned a lukewarm reception in the poll. Overall, 42% either somewhat or strongly support the program, 38% somewhat or strongly oppose it, with 14% offering no opinion. The payments were sent to single tax filers making up to $50,000 a year, $75,000 for head of household or $100,000 for married, filing jointly. The program cost about $155 million, with the money coming from the state’s Budget Stabilization Fund, also known as the rainy-day fund. Finally, UNH released new polling this week on President Donald Trump. It shows 62% of Maine residents disapprove of Trump’s overall job as president, 37% approve and 1 % are unsure. Second District Democrat Matt Dunlap says the federal government needs to do more to protect consumers. The comments came Wednesday at a town hall in Lewiston. The New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Sienna survey shows Sen. Susan Collins with a narrow lead over Democrat Troy Jackson. Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie stumped for Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles during the event. A former defense contractor alleges he traded campaign contributions for federal contracts.

title: New UNH poll shows Democrat Amanada Janoo gaining on Gov. Phil Scott - WPTZ
content: Democratic nominee for governor, Amanda Janoo, has significantly increased her support since winning the Democratic primary, according to a new UNH poll. The overall poll shows 49% of voters would support Janoo if the election was held today, and 43% of voters would support Phil Scott. 882 likely Vermont voters completed the survey. Of them, 60% self-identified as Democrats, and 31% identified as Republicans. There is no party registration in Vermont, so there's limited data on how many Democrats and Republicans there are in the state. The Independent Voter Project reports 53.1% of registered voters selected the Democratic primary ballot, and only 20.4% of voters selected the Republican party ballot in 2026. Some voters who identify as Republican may have selected the Democratic primary ballot, as some state offices had no Republican challenger. title: Fast-growing life sciences sector looks to colleges to keep pace - NH Business Review
content: New Hampshire’s life sciences industry is expanding quickly, but the workers employers need range far beyond biomedical scientists — from manufacturing technicians and engineers to project managers, supply-chain specialists and finance professionals. At the Empower Life Sciences event hosted by NH Life Sciences (NHLS) at the University of New Hampshire Durham on Sept. 9, employers and educators argued the state may already have much of that talent. The problem is connecting people, programs and employers quickly enough. Moderator Cindy Conde, co-founder of NH Life Sciences, makes a comment during a “demand side” panel, which featured Theresa Edick of BA Sciences; Jean-Paul Ouellette of Lonza; Dan Harris of HiArc; and Conor Cullinane of Pirouette Pharma during Empower Life Sciences in Durham on Sept. 9. (Photo by Sarah Pearson) “We don’t have a talent problem,” said Matt Simon, executive director of UNH’s Biotech Innovation Center and ReGen Valley Common Campus. “We have a talent alignment problem for the life sciences.” Simon cited recent data from the New Hampshire Department of Employment Security that overall private-sector employment grew 4% from 2019 to 2025. During that same period, employment in the core life sciences sector grew 24%. “Higher education wasn’t built to respond to that level of growth,” he said. Simon was among the speakers on a “supply side” panel, along with UNH professors Sherine Elsawa, chair of the UNH College of Life Sciences and Agriculture; AI specialist Samuel Carton of the UNH College of Engineering and Physical Sciences; and Peter Lane of the UNH Paul School of Business and Economics. The “demand side” panel featured industry representatives Theresa Edick of BA Sciences, Dan Harris of HiArc, Jean-Paul Ouellette of Lonza and Conor Cullinane of  Pirouette Pharma. “Our needs are great and wide, I would say, which puts Lonza in a particularly interesting position because the site continues to grow,”  Ouellette said. The Portsmouth location currently employs about 2,400. “We’ll be adding another 300 to 400 people by the end of 2027.” Ouellette said the site’s workforce is roughly divided in thirds among manufacturing, quality and testing and support service functions. Through its developing Pirouette Academy, new hires at Pirouette Pharma will rotate through different roles to understand the full product development process, Cullinane said. Panelists also emphasized transferable skills such as adaptability, communication, problem-solving and critical thinking so that graduates have skills to adapt to changing technologies over their careers. Hands-on coursework, internships and other experiential learning give students opportunities to practice those skills. “Too often, workforce development is interpreted as ‘We have these immediate openings. Can you help us fill them?’ To me, that’s too late,” Lane said. “We need to have these ongoing conversations. Yes, we’ll help you fill your short-term needs, but help us understand what your needs are going to be in three to five years. … Then you set up this feedback loop where we try to do a better job of anticipating.” As an industry association, NHLS sees itself as a convener and connector. “We told our members, ‘We want you to engage. We want you to start these conversations to build a relationship with the university,’ ” said NHLS President Andrea Hechavarria, in her opening remarks. “We have an extraordinary opportunity in front of us.” Research and development activity is driving momentum in the New Hampshire life sciences industry, as this slide at Empower Life Sciences touts during the Sept. 9 meeting in Durham. (Photo by Sarah Pearson) In conversation with Hechavarria, UNH President Elizabeth Chilton said UNH has identified health and life sciences as a strategic priority, and its federally supported biomedical research has tripled to more than $14 million in the last seven years. More than 50 life sciences firms have recruited from UNH in the past five years, and the university is expanding partnerships in research, internships, commercialization and professional development. UNH is also betting that physical proximity between companies, researchers and students can help strengthen those relationships. Chilton highlighted a development project the university broke ground on this spring. UNH is developing The Edge, a 43-acre community of combined research space, housing and retail. The university envisions it as a better way to connect students with companies seeking talent. As construction continues, the university is planning additional research buildings designed around companies’ specific needs. “The Edge can’t be built fast enough,” Hechavarria said. “I think it’s the secret sauce. It’s that live-work-play environment that everyone seeks and is hungry for.” New Hampshire’s life sciences industry is expanding quickly, but the workers employers need range far beyond biomedical scientists — from manufacturing technicians and engineers to project managers, supply-chain specialists and finance professionals. title: UNH tradition goes up in smoke as Harvard triumphs - The New Hampshire
content: On Sept. 19, 2026, the University of New Hampshire’s Wildcat football team hosted the Harvard Crimson in Wildcat Stadium. Unfortunately for the home team, the Crimson were an astounding 17-point favorite. The Wildcats did an excellent job of shutting down the veteran Crimson offense in the first quarter. By the end of the first, the upset looked extremely promising. In addition to the hopeful win, the Wildcat fans got hyped for the annual chalk toss, held every year at the beginning of the Wildcat football season. The Cat Pack, made up of both students and alumni, have participated in this hype event for decades, and if tradition continues, hopefully many more to come. The chalk toss was initiated by the Cat Pack leaders, where they handed out handfuls of ‘chalk’ to the participants, waited for the countdown, and threw the smokey handfuls into the air to get pumped up for the game, to bring the UNH community together, and to bring victory to UNH. Shortly after however, the Wildcat’s hype train wore off quickly as the Crimson opened the second quarter with a 1-yard touchdown (TD). With their first redzone opportunity, the Wildcats stayed in the game with a rushing TD, but their fire went out quickly after the Harvard 20-yard option reverse touchdown, which extended their lead to 7. Shortly after, a brutal interception in their own territory in the final 20 seconds of the half brought the Crimson back into the redzone, which led to a two-score lead. The Wildcats headed back into the locker room, heads hung low, down 21-7. The Crimson got the ball after half, the Wildcat defence looked fierce and they forced the Crimson to either punt or try to go up another three. Fortunately for the Wildcats, the career-long field goal came up just short. The teams traded interceptions, ending in a Harvard field goal, which set the score 24-7. With defeat already in sight, the Wildcats went three-and-out which ultimately caused another Crimson TD. The teams traded possessions until Harvard took a knee, winning the game 31-7. Sadly, tradition wasn’t enough for the Wildcats to get the victory. Maybe next week the Wildcats can get the win when they travel to play Sacred Heart, who is currently 0-2.

title: Investing in discovery - University of New Hampshire
content: From left: Nathan Furey, Wilfred Wollheim, Analena Bruce An endowed professorship is a quiet piece of ‌academic infrastructure, like a stone bridge that ‌outlasts the traffic crossing it. Funded in perpetuity, it frees professors from the constant pull of short-term funding cycles so they can pursue questions whose answers may take years to emerge. The endowment supports not only an individual faculty member but also the students, laboratories, field sites, and ideas that surround them. Donors who fund endowed professorships create a lasting legacy that’s tied to their values and experiences. It’s a meaningful way to give back and stay connected to the university — with recognition, pride, and the satisfaction of making a long-term impact. Nathan Furey, associate professor in the department of biological sciences, has been named the first Robert Summers Professor of Biology, a new professorship established through a $1 million gift from philanthropist Robert Summers. The award recognizes Furey’s internationally respected research in aquatic animal movement and his commitment to graduate student mentorship. Funding from the professorship will support student research opportunities, fieldwork, conference travel, and innovative projects that advance scientific discovery. The generous gift reflects Summers’ long-standing interest in advancing scientific inquiry and education and his aim to strengthen the academic environment for both faculty and graduate students in the life sciences. Wilfred Wollheim, professor in the department of natural resources and the environment, has been awarded the Josephine A. Lamprey Professorship in Climate and Sustainability. Wollheim’s research focuses on how freshwater ecosystems respond to climate change, land use, and human activity, helping communities better protect water quality and aquatic systems. The professorship will support continued research and collaboration aimed at advancing sustainable, science-based solutions to climate and environmental challenges in New Hampshire and beyond. Analena Bruce, associate professor in the department of agriculture, nutrition, and food systems, has been named the Thomas W. Haas Professor in Sustainable Food Systems. The professorship supports efforts to strengthen sustainable, equitable, and resilient food systems across New Hampshire and New England. Bruce plans to expand partnerships with farmers, community organizations, and food system leaders through research, outreach, and collaboration focused on improving farm viability and access to healthy food. title: Do birds spread harmful bacteria on dairy farms? - University of New Hampshire
content: Andrea Ayala, assistant professor of natural resources and the environment, is studying  the role small birds play in transmitting Campylobacter jejuni — a bacterium that can affect herd health and cause foodborne illness in humans — to cows at dairy farms in New Hampshire and across the U.S. Early observations indicate that house sparrows likely play a much larger role in the spread of Campylobacter and other bacteria harmful to animal health than previously thought. Dairy cows are known to carry Campylobacter, though not at levels that pose a health threat. But sparrows can carry additional Campylobacter populations that tip the balance toward infection. If confirmed, the findings would reinforce the value of vaccinating cows against Campylobacter infection and installing netting to keep the birds away from barns and feed storage areas. “If we can show clearly that sparrows are initiating Campylobacter infections in cows, it demonstrates to farmers that mitigation strategies are well worth it,” says Ayala. There are more than 20 species of Campylobacter, but Ayala is focused on C. jejuni because of its impact on human, animal, and environmental health. The research is funded by the NH Agricultural Experiment Station. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Team at work - University of New Hampshire
content: The UNH College of Life Sciences and Agriculture associate deans, under the leadership of Dean Anthony S. Davis, are rooted in their shared commitment to the college’s land-grant mission and public higher education. Whether they’re supporting student success, advancing research, building partnerships, or strengthening communities across New Hampshire, they care deeply about the people and work that drive COLSA’s impact and advance its mission. Kimberly J. Babbitt ’84Associate DeanDirector of Sustainability Programs With her thoughtful and collaborative leadership style, Kimberly J. Babbitt guides both operational priorities and sustainability initiatives across the college. She’s known for building strong relationships, connecting people across disciplines, and helping teams move complex projects forward with clarity and purpose. In her role, Babbitt works to support programs and partnerships that advance environmental stewardship, community resilience, and long-term sustainability both at the college and the broader university. She enjoys bringing people together around shared goals and helping create solutions that have a meaningful impact for students, communities, and the environment. “What makes COLSA so distinctive is the way we connect discovery, education, and service,” says Babbitt. “Our students and faculty aren't just studying today's challenges — they're developing practical and sustainable solutions that strengthen the environment, economy, and quality of life in New Hampshire and around the world.” Jesse Stabile Morrell ’99, ’04G, ’13GAssociate Dean for Academic Affairs Jesse Stabile Morrell is deeply invested in creating an academic experience where students feel supported, challenged, and connected. Known for her student-centered approach, she works closely with faculty, staff, and students to help shape programs and opportunities — like the college’s new TRAIL Network (read about it on p. 17) — that prepare graduates for careers that are both meaningful and adaptable in a rapidly changing world. Morrell cares deeply about experiential learning and believes some of the most impactful learning happens outside of traditional classroom settings, whether that’s through research, internships, fieldwork, or collaborative projects. Her leadership style emphasizes mentorship, accessibility, and helping students build confidence alongside knowledge. “COLSA is a special community where the faculty and staff are talented, hardworking, and dedicated to the success of each and every student,” says Morrell. “I’m grateful each day to work with such a special and committed group.” Anton BekkermanAssociate Dean for ResearchDirector, New Hampshire Agricultural Experiment Station Anton Bekkerman brings curiosity, collaboration, and big-picture thinking to his roles as associate dean for research and director of the New Hampshire Agricultural Experiment Station. With a background in agricultural economics and applied research, he enjoys connecting ideas across disciplines and finding ways research can make a tangible difference for communities in New Hampshire and beyond. Much of Bekkerman’s work centers on building partnerships and supporting research that tackles real-world challenges related to agriculture, food systems, sustainability, and the environment. He’s also focused on creating opportunities for students to get involved in hands-on research and experiential learning that prepares them for meaningful careers after graduation. “It has been rewarding to see a number of the goals set four to five years ago — growing the impacts of our locally inspired research, better supporting the education and careers of our students, having stronger connections to our state's communities — become successes,” says Bekkerman. “The collective efforts of our faculty, staff, and students have resulted in a foundation from which we can set much bigger goals. Knowing that we can not only set but achieve those goals is really exciting.” Amy LoaderAssociate Dean Director, UNH Cooperative Extension Amy Loader is passionate about connecting people with practical, research-based knowledge that improves lives and strengthens communities across New Hampshire. As associate dean and director of UNH Cooperative Extension, she partners with faculty, staff, students, and community members to advance education, outreach, and public engagement statewide. With a background in agriculture, environmental stewardship, and organizational leadership, Loader brings a thoughtful, collaborative approach to her work. She values strong relationships and believes Extension’s greatest impact comes from listening to communities, understanding their needs, and connecting them with trusted expertise. A proud COLSA alumna, Loader finds deep meaning in seeing graduates apply their education to support New Hampshire’s people, food systems, and natural resources. title: Getting to the root of why students leave STEM - University of New Hampshire
content: Research at UNH is seeking to understand why many college students abandon STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) subjects for other fields of study and how undergraduate programs can improve student engagement and retention. Given employer needs for highly skilled and technologically proficient workers in the Granite State and beyond, STEM training that meets workplace demands is critical. Melissa Aikens, associate professor of biological sciences, studies how to improve undergraduate biology education, analyzing both teaching methods and how students respond. The field, known as discipline-based education research, is relatively new. Gateway courses can be key for STEM student retention, and Aikens puts her own research insights into action when she teaches introductory biology each fall. Group work and peer-led team learning have both been shown to lead to better student outcomes, so she works to incorporate these activities into her introductory class. “We know that group work and peer support tend to lead to better outcomes,” says Aikens. “We now need to do a deeper dive into how and why they do.” While research can be challenging in what remains a small field, Aikens is quick to praise UNH’s environment and support for her work. “The field’s motto is ‘show me the data,’ as it progresses beyond anecdotal observations in the classroom to showing the mechanisms underlying them,” she says. “I’m looking to bring the latest findings to our own classrooms and teaching practices here at UNH.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: A new tool promises to expand research capability - University of New Hampshire
content: The right tool can make all the difference. That’s the case for a new instrument at UNH: an automated isothermal titration calorimeter (ITC), whose applications include optimizing drug development, improving chemical removal in the environment, and helping create materials that accelerate wound healing. Isothermal titration calorimetry measures whether heat is consumed or released when two things — such as two chemicals, two solutions, or two biological molecules — are mixed and the magnitude of the change over time. It sounds simple, but it has far-reaching applications. “It greatly enhances our capacity for exciting research at UNH and beyond,” says Sean Edington, assistant professor in the department of molecular, cellular, and biomedical sciences and the department of chemistry, who spearheaded the effort to secure funding for the ITC from the National Science Foundation. “It also provides our students with an important research skill, whether they continue with academic research or move into the biotech industry.” The ITC, housed at UNH's University Instrumentation Center, is accessible for both UNH and external academic users, as well as nonacademic users as capacity permits, expanding capabilities across organizations in different fields. Acquiring the ITC was an interdisciplinary effort that included Aylin Aykanat, Nate Oldenhuis, Linqing Li, Roy Planalp, and Patricia Stone from the UNH College of Engineering and Physical Sciences and Eva Rose Balog from the University of New England. title: A tiny sensor could make a big impact for New Hampshire's dairy farms - University of New Hampshire
content: UNH researchers Claira Seely and Sarah Allen are partnering with the Grafton County Farm to determine if a small 4-inch capsule could help small dairy operations in New Hampshire become more efficient and productive. The new technology, made by smaXtec, is called a bolus. It is placed in the cow’s stomach, where it does not cause harm or discomfort and remains for the duration of her life, measuring key health indicators, including body temperature, rumination, activity, hydration, and feed patterns. The collected data can be used to inform cost-effective herd management, nutrition, and labor decisions, as well as detect illness even before a cow shows symptoms. These data-driven decisions could be a real boon for New Hampshire’s dairy producers, who don’t have the same ability as larger farms to absorb unexpected or unnecessary expenses, notes Seely, an assistant professor in the department of agriculture, nutrition, and food systems. “Most people want the smaller farms to succeed,” says Allen, an Extension state specialist in dairy production. “These monitoring systems are another way to help keep small farms in business, which is good for all of our communities.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: Fostering biomedical research excellence - University of New Hampshire
content: I‌t is hard to overstate the impact ‌that the Center of Integrated ‌Biomedical and Bioengineering Research (CIBBR) has had at UNH since its establishment in 2017. The statistics are impressive on their own: 19 tenure-track faculty hired, $23.8 million awarded to CIBBR principal investigators, $3.2 million invested in research infrastructure, and 256 publications to date. But for Rick Cote, who spearheaded CIBBR’s formation and led it as director for nearly a decade, the numbers do not fully capture the center’s most important achievements. “For me, one major accomplishment of CIBBR has been implementing the mentoring program that we provide for our early-stage researchers,” says Cote, a professor of biochemistry and molecular biology who stepped down from the directorship this year. “The CIBBR leadership team takes pride in working closely with them and helping them to successfully apply for major grants and to advance their research careers.” CIBBR has also catalyzed interdisciplinary research across traditional academic silos. Researchers in the College of Engineering and Physical Sciences (CEPS) regularly collaborate with COLSA researchers to carry out research projects that span basic biomedical and bioengineering disciplines. “A great example is the work by Sarah Walker, who is a cancer researcher and an expert in mammalian cell culture,” says Cote. “Working with Linqing Li in CEPS, she’s using engineered scaffolds to grow cancer cells in a three-dimensional environment to mimic how they grow in the body rather than on a flat dish.” The story of CIBBR’s inception begins many years before it came into existence. Historically, UNH had been very successful at attracting funding from federal agencies such as NASA and NSF, but the National Institutes of Health (NIH) was a notable exception. Early conversations between Cote and Jan Nisbet, then the senior vice provost for research, focused on how to improve NIH grant success. The conversations led to the launch of an NIH grant-writing program (UP-2-NIH) that continues to this day. Two other developments also set the stage. First, a reorganization in COLSA included the formation of the department of molecular, cellular, and biomedical sciences (MCBS), a department that included a focus on growing biomedical research at UNH. Around the same time, CEPS saw opportunities in the biomedical research space and created its successful bioengineering undergraduate degree program. With the pieces in place, Cote teamed with Kelley Thomas, fellow MCBS professor and the director of UNH’s Hubbard Center for Genome Studies, on a successful grant application to the National Institute of General Medical Sciences’ Centers of Biomedical Research Excellence (COBRE) program to form CIBBR and begin Phase One of three planned five-year phases. “One critical element to our success was the strong institutional commitments we received from around UNH,” says Cote. “The Office of Research and Innovation is committed to helping build the research infrastructure we needed, and the deans were willing to commit to hiring biomedical and bioengineering faculty to build a critical mass of researchers.” The other members of CIBBR’s original leadership team — Thomas, Don Wojchowski, and Steve Fiering, professor of microbiology and immunology at Dartmouth College’s Geisel School of Medicine — are still in their roles. Wojchowski, also a professor in MCBS, leads the molecular and cellular phenotyping core that has acquired a suite of instruments for shared use, some of which are housed and managed by the staff of the University Instrumentation Center. Thomas leads the data science core that addresses the strong need at UNH for a single place to go for statistical, bioinformatics, research computing infrastructure, and other services related to working with large datasets, while Fiering oversees the mentoring program. Now, CIBBR is preparing to enter a new phase in more ways than one. It is wrapping up Phase Two, and the leadership team has been joined by Alexei Tulin, an expert in epigenetics and cancer biology who came to UNH from the University of North Dakota, who is taking over as director of CIBBR as it gears up for Phase Three. Cote expects that the next five years will see a greater emphasis on building the research infrastructure along with a business model needed to support UNH biomedical research once COBRE support ends. “Our goal is to ensure that the research programs and instrumentation supported by CIBBR will have a lasting impact in promoting interdisciplinary biomedical research at UNH that leads to enhancing human health,” says Cote.
